title: Study notes
html:
Plain film of the acute abdomen

  • Pneumoperitoneum: air crescent under the diaphragm on an upright film (or left lateral decubitus), Rigler sign; causes – perforated ulcer, diverticulitis, post-operative. CT is more sensitive.
  • Obstruction: dilated loops with air–fluid levels above the obstacle.

Barium studies – the vocabulary

Indications: chronic conditions, post-operative anatomy and function, findings on other exams. Contraindications: perforation and acute inflammation – use water-soluble iodine instead.

  • Achalasia: dilated oesophagus, air–fluid level, absent gastric bubble, short smooth tapered bird's beak.
  • Benign stricture: axial, long, regular, progressive (peptic, caustic). Cancer: eccentric, short, irregular, abrupt shoulders, filling defects.
  • Hiatal hernia: sliding (junction above the diaphragm) vs rolling/para-oesophageal (junction below, fundus beside the oesophagus) vs mixed.
  • Colon: cancer = apple-core stenosis; diverticulosis = multiple addition images; ulcerative colitis = continuous from rectum, lead-pipe; Crohn = skip lesions, cobblestone, string sign, fistulas.

Liver

  • US: steatosis and fibrosis hyperechoic (bright liver); acute hepatitis/congestion hypoechoic; cirrhosis = nodular surface, caudate hypertrophy, portal hypertension (splenomegaly, ascites, collaterals). HCC surveillance = US every 6 months.
  • Characterisation by enhancement pattern (see curves): haemangioma peripheral nodular centripetal; FNH arterial + central scar, bright on hepatobiliary phase; HCC wash-in/wash-out; metastases (the most frequent malignant lesions in a non-cirrhotic liver) usually multiple, hypo in the portal phase, can be cystic.
  • Hydatid cyst: membranes, daughter cysts, calcified wall. Abscess: thick wall, debris, air.

Biliary tree and pancreas

  • Normal: intrahepatic ducts < 2 mm (not visible), CBD ≤ 7 mm, gallbladder wall ≤ 3–4 mm. US = best for gallstones (echogenic, shadow, mobile); MRCP for duct stones and strictures; double-duct sign = pancreatic head tumour.
  • Acute pancreatitis: contrast CT at 48–72 h for necrosis and collections (not for diagnosis). Chronic: calcifications, moniliform Wirsung, atrophy, pseudocysts; focal form mimics cancer.
  • Pancreatic adenocarcinoma: hypodense, hypovascular mass, upstream duct dilatation, vascular encasement.

Exam reflexes

  • Iodinated contrast is not mandatory for occlusion or pneumoperitoneum, but is needed to characterise a liver nodule.
  • Gadoxetic acid is not used to detect haemangiomas.
  • Entero-MRI needs fluid-distended, immobile bowel.
